title: Software engineer situations
authored: Project-authored reflective scenarios (2026-10-23). Not a validated situational judgment test; there are no correct answers.

scenarios.title: Reviewing a senior's pull request
scenarios.prompt: A principal engineer asks you to review their large pull request. You spot what looks like a race condition, but you are not completely sure.

options.text: Leave a clear comment describing the race and how to reproduce it.
Ask a question in the review: 'Could this run concurrently here?'
Message them privately before commenting publicly.
Approve; they have far more context than you do.

scenarios.title: Rewrite temptation
scenarios.prompt: You are asked to add a small feature to a legacy module that you find painful to read. You believe a rewrite would take a week.

options.text: Add the feature with minimal changes and leave the module alone.
Rewrite the module as part of the feature; it will pay off.
Add characterization tests first, then refactor only the part you touch.
Add the feature, then pitch a rewrite with a short write-up.

scenarios.title: Unclear ticket
scenarios.prompt: A ticket says 'make export faster'. There is no target, no dataset and no owner listed.

options.text: Profile the export, fix the biggest bottleneck and report the gain.
Ask the reporter for a target time and a sample dataset before touching code.
Bring it to refinement so the team can clarify it together.
Spend an hour measuring, then propose a target to the reporter.

scenarios.title: Pairing with a junior
scenarios.prompt: You are pairing with a junior engineer who is slow but eager. The task would take you half the time alone.

options.text: Let them drive and guide with questions, accepting the slower pace.
Drive yourself and explain as you go.
Split the task: you take the hard part, they take a well-defined piece.
Agree a learning goal for the session and timebox it.

scenarios.title: Noisy alerts
scenarios.prompt: Your on-call rotation receives dozens of alerts a week that need no action. Everyone complains but nobody fixes it.

options.text: Spend your next on-call week tuning or deleting the noisiest alerts.
Propose an alert review policy with owners and a monthly cleanup.
Raise it with the team lead so it gets prioritised properly.
Mute the obvious ones locally and get on with your work.

scenarios.title: Choosing a library
scenarios.prompt: You need a date-handling library. One is popular and heavy; another is small, elegant and maintained by one person.

options.text: Choose the popular one; maintenance risk matters more than size.
Choose the small one; it fits better and can be vendored if abandoned.
Compare both on a short checklist: licence, activity, size, API.
Use the standard library and write the small helpers you need.

scenarios.title: Late performance regression
scenarios.prompt: The day before a release, you notice your feature makes a key page 30 percent slower in staging.

options.text: Tell the release owner now and suggest holding your feature back.
Work late to optimise it before the release.
Ship it behind a flag that is off by default.
Ship it; staging is not production and users may not notice.

scenarios.title: Disagreeing with the architect
scenarios.prompt: The architect mandates an event-driven design for a service you think would be simpler as a plain CRUD API.

options.text: Write a short comparison and ask for a decision meeting.
Raise your concern once, then build what was decided.
Build the simpler version as a spike to show the difference.
Follow the mandate; consistency across services has its own value.

scenarios.title: Asked to skip tests
scenarios.prompt: Your lead suggests skipping tests for a feature to hit a demo date, promising time afterwards.

options.text: Refuse to skip them for the risky paths, but drop the rest.
Agree and create a ticket for the missing tests right away.
Write the tests anyway, even if it means working late.
Agree; the demo is what matters right now.

scenarios.title: Knowledge silo
scenarios.prompt: You are the only person who understands the billing integration. You are going on holiday for two weeks.

options.text: Write a runbook and walk a teammate through it before you leave.
Stay reachable by phone in case anything breaks.
Leave notes in the repository README and trust the team.
Ask your lead to arrange cover; it is a team problem.

scenarios.title: Refactor inside a feature
scenarios.prompt: While implementing a feature, you see a refactor that would clean up three other call sites.

options.text: Do it in the same pull request; it is related.
Do it in a separate pull request first, then build the feature on top.
Note it in a ticket and stay focused on the feature.
Ask the team whether they want it before doing anything.

scenarios.title: AI-generated code in review
scenarios.prompt: A teammate submits a large pull request that was clearly generated by an AI assistant. It passes tests, but parts look unfamiliar to them when you ask.

options.text: Ask them to walk you through it and to remove anything they cannot explain.
Review it like any other code; tests pass and that is what matters.
Suggest splitting it into smaller pull requests that are easier to understand.
Raise a team discussion about guidelines for AI-assisted changes.
